statement: For $N$ random variables $X_1, \ldots, X_N$ represented as a random vector $\mathbf{X} = (X_1, \ldots, X_N)^T$, the joint distribution is defined by the joint cumulative distribution function $F_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname{P}(X_1 \leq x_1, \ldots, X_N \leq x_N)$, which specifies the probability that each random variable $X_i$ simultaneously takes a value less than or equal to $x_i$. For discrete random variables, it is characterized by the joint probability mass function $p_{X_1, \ldots, X_n}(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = \mathrm{P}(X_1=x_1, \ldots, X_n=x_n)$; for continuous random variables, it is given by the joint probability density function $f_{X_1, \ldots, X_n}(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ defined as the derivative of the joint cumulative distribution function.

symbols.meaning: Random vector $(X_1, \ldots, X_N)^T$ of $N$ random variables
Joint cumulative distribution function of random vector $\mathbf{X}$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}$
Joint probability mass function of two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$
Joint probability density function of two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$
Marginal probability density function of random variable $X$
Marginal probability density function of random variable $Y$

properties.property: For discrete random variables, the joint probabilities sum to 1 over all possible outcome combinations: $\sum_i \sum_j \dots \sum_k \mathrm{P}(X_1=x_{1i}, X_2=x_{2j}, \dots, X_n=x_{nk}) = 1$.
properties.why: The probability of some combination of outcomes occurring across the entire space is necessarily 1.

properties.property: For continuous random variables, the integral of the joint probability density function over all coordinates is 1: $\int_{x_1} \dots \int_{x_n} f_{X_1, \ldots, X_n}(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \, dx_n \ldots dx_1 = 1$.
properties.why: The total probability assigned by the density across the continuous domain equals 1.

properties.property: Marginal distributions are determined from the joint distribution by integrating or summing over the other variables: $f_X(x) = \int f_{X,Y}(x,y) \, dy$ and $f_Y(y) = \int f_{X,Y}(x,y) \, dx$.
properties.why: Integrating the joint density over all values of $Y$ leaves the unconditional density of $X$.

properties.property: The joint distribution expands into conditional and marginal distributions via the chain rule of probability: $p_{X_1, \ldots, X_n}(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = \mathrm{P}(X_1=x_1) \cdot \mathrm{P}(X_2=x_2 \mid X_1=x_1) \cdots \mathrm{P}(X_n=x_n \mid X_1=x_1, \ldots, X_{n-1}=x_{n-1})$.
properties.why: Joint probabilities factor iteratively into successive conditional probabilities.

properties.property: Random variables are independent if and only if the joint distribution factorizes into the product of marginal distributions: $F_{X,Y}(x,y) = F_X(x) \cdot F_Y(y)$ (CDFs), $P(X=x \text{ and } Y=y) = P(X=x) \cdot P(Y=y)$ (PMFs), or $f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x) \cdot f_Y(y)$ (PDFs).
properties.why: Knowledge of the value of one variable leaves the conditional distribution of the other identical to its unconditional marginal distribution.

properties.property: For mixed continuous and discrete variables, the mixed joint density $f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)\mathrm{P}(Y=y) = \mathrm{P}(Y=y \mid X=x)f_X(x)$ allows recovering the joint CDF via $F_{X,Y}(x,y) = \sum_{t \leq y} \int_{-\infty}^x f_{X,Y}(s,t) \, ds$.
properties.why: The density is taken with respect to the product measure on the respective supports of the continuous and discrete variables.

assumptions.assumption: All random variables in the joint distribution are defined on the same underlying probability space.
assumptions.breaks_when: Variables are defined across disparate or incompatible outcome spaces where joint events $(X_1 \leq x_1, \ldots, X_N \leq x_N)$ are not meaningfully defined.

assumptions.assumption: For continuous random variables, the joint cumulative distribution function is differentiable.
assumptions.breaks_when: The distribution has discrete mass points or singular continuous parts, causing the derivative $f_{X,Y}$ to not exist everywhere or fail to integrate to 1.

failure_modes.mode: Attempting to assign a pure PMF or PDF to a mixed discrete-continuous pair of variables
failure_modes.signature: Cannot collectively assign either a probability density function or a probability mass function to $(X,Y)$
failure_modes.cause: One variable is discrete and the other is continuous, requiring a mixed joint density defined with respect to the product measure.

failure_modes.mode: Factoring joint distribution directly into product of marginals for dependent variables
failure_modes.cause: The variables are dependent, so conditioning alters their distributions and the simple product rule fails.

failure_modes.mode: Using covariance to determine dependence structure when relationship is nonlinear
failure_modes.signature: $\operatorname{cov}(X,Y) = 0$ despite $X$ and $Y$ having strong statistical dependence
failure_modes.cause: Covariance measures only the linear relationship between variables and may be insensitive to nonlinear dependencies.
